title: How do you deal with the backlash against AI-assisted artwork in your games?
author: sarmatianheroes
selftext:
I'm a solo developer working on Sarmatian Heroes, a historical turn-based strategy game inspired by Heroes of Might and Magic.

Yesterday, I shared my gameplay trailer on r/HoMM, hoping to get some feedback on the gameplay mechanics. While I received some genuinely useful feedback and positive comments, a significant part of the discussion ended up being about AI-generated artwork rather than gameplay.

You can see the trailer and the original discussion in the linked Reddit post.

I've spent thousands of hours developing the game. All animations are made manually by me, environmental elements are procedurally generated without AI, and the artwork is a combination of AI-assisted, handmade and marketplace assets.

I'm curious about your experiences as developers:

* Do you receive similar reactions when presenting your games outside AI-friendly communities?
* Have you noticed a significant impact on player interest or Steam wishlists?
* Do you think this negativity is primarily a Reddit phenomenon, or does it reflect the broader gaming audience?
* Has it affected your development or marketing decisions?

Here's my game on Steam if you'd like to see what I'm working on:

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/5222130/Sarmatian\_Heroes/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5222130/Sarmatian_Heroes/)

I'd love to hear your experiences, especially from developers who have already released commercial games using AI-assisted artwork.

comments.author: Commercial-Ad9859
comments.body:
I’m a solo developer who relies heavily on AI throughout my entire development pipeline, not just for artwork.  
Last week, I showcased one of my games at a physical gaming expo in Sweden. What struck me was how different the experience was compared to online discussions. People were playing, laughing, competing and asking questions about the game itself.  
However, I also had conversations with industry professionals who raised legitimate concerns about AI, particularly regarding publishing, public perception and legal uncertainty.  
I think there’s an important distinction between how players experience a game and how people perceive its production process. Both matter, but they’re not necessarily the same.  
I haven’t released a commercial game yet, so I can’t comment on sales or wishlist conversion. But my experience at the expo was genuinely encouraging.  
My approach going forward is to remain transparent about my development process, continuously improve the quality of my work and let the games speak for themselves.  
You don’t have to convince everyone that AI-assisted development is legitimate. Your responsibility is to make a game worth playing.  
Best of luck with Sarmatian Heroes!

Thanks! The game has a lot of interconnected mechanics, and even individual artifacts introduce new gameplay mechanics rather than just increasing stats. Balancing all these interactions takes a lot of time, mainly through repeatedly playing, testing and refining the game. That's something AI can't do for me.

I've also spent a considerable amount of time manually optimizing the code and rendering performance. My goal is to make the game consume as little battery as possible on laptops and run smoothly without requiring a dedicated GPU.

But that was my vision for the project from the beginning. I wanted to create a game with this level of mechanical depth while keeping the hardware requirements very low, knowing full well how much work it would involve.

I worked in game development a decade ago, long before generative AI became a thing, so I knew what I was getting myself into. :D

replies.author: sarmatianheroes
replies.body:
I actually have around 20 years of programming experience and work as a software architect. About a decade ago, I developed mobile games for a company as the sole programmer, working alongside artists, and could build an entire game in a month. And that was without generative AI, as these tools simply didn't exist back then.

But developing a strategy game with this level of mechanical depth is a completely different challenge compared to making a platformer or a simple mobile game.

Every new mechanic interacts with existing ones, so the complexity grows exponentially rather than linearly. You have to consider how each new mechanic affects the others, test those interactions and balance the entire system.

Writing the code is only part of the work. Designing, playtesting, balancing and refining all these interconnected mechanics takes a huge amount of time, and AI doesn't magically solve those problems.

  
There is over 1k of imgs files (counting sprites as single), 300k LOC, including over 50k lines of just game definitions in jsons...

comments.author: 2ko2ko2
comments.body:
If you've spent 1000s of hours on it, and only some of the artwork has been touched with AI, why not just replace those few assets with marketplace or handmade items like the rest?

Although Reddit is especially hostile towards AI, Steam isn't much better. Only a handful of games made.with AI have "made it" (generated more revenue than the devs put in), and most of them only use AI in the coding and marketing materials (which according to surveys, of the Anti AI crowd are the most accepted uses). Only 1 I can think of (Slotbound) used AI for artwork as well, and it only did so well because the majority of the sales came from Asia where anti-ai sentiment is much, much lower.

For a niche game like this, you really are going to be relying on the type of people who frequent reddit subs and community forums about it to take interest. It's not like HoMM is a raking in cash, it's a small franchise with a dedicated fanbase. And if the community's reaction towards AI art is that negative, it might be worth looking into getting it replaced if it is a game you are hoping to be commercially viable (still might sink. It just gives you a better shot).

If this is just a passion project though cause you love HoMM, and you don't want to spend more time and money than you already have, then I guess it doesn't matter if they play it or not. Ignore them lol

comments.author: Underdriven
comments.body:
As someone on the fence about AI, what people really care about is the outsourcing of the artistry to an AI. I haven't seen one good argument against the outsourcing of tedium and code-writing to an AI. 

What people want is for you to prove to them that you are capable of producing it without AI, that you haven't killed anyone's income, and that you have bettered your own faculties in the process. I don't think there is any reasonable way to do that.

We are moving towards a sort of two-market system with AI in the art world: Art as an experience and art as a form of expression. It's going to be a generation or two until we see people treat AI artwork more often than not as a form of human expression.

What I'm saying is that I don't think you should put too much energy into trying to make people be ok with your work unless you really want to go into every ai -assisted asset and change those amendments by drawing over it yourself.

Well that's debatable. Those are all up in the air for a lot of these cases. 
 But I agree with the degree of work involved. I believe that the scalable nature of what's ok with AI art in comparison to human made art allows for people to have their work validated when using AI. I simply believe that AI should allow people to think more about and on the things they actually want to while the mindless drudgery is outsourced. Ideally I would see people generally using their brains MORE rather than less. Not that it's exactly pertinent to the topic, but we need to get the next generation(s) on track with responsible AI usage, because there are breathtakingly worrying trends emerging.

replies.author: Underdriven

I think it's just down to a lack of transparency and perhaps some moral ignorance/irresponsibility. It's hard to compare the two fields. Especially when there are a great many people who have a rather principled view of art as an eternal avenue of human expression. Personally, I'm dismayed by any loss of agency or occupation that comes at the hands of AI, so the people involved in seeing their fields collapse have my sympathathies equally, but if you were to ask me what I'd rather save, then id immediately save art.

However, I'm not sure yet that I have to think about saving anything, as my general forecast sees human-Art still sit in a distinct place for humanity moving on.

replies.author: Inevitable_Secret186
replies.body:
"What people want is for you to prove to them that you are capable of producing it without AI, that you haven't killed anyone's income, and that you have bettered your own faculties in the process. I don't think there is any reasonable way to do that."

People don't care at all about the morality of it despite what you see posted on reddit. In a few years everything will be made with AI, and the people complaining will be using it themselves. Sure, people will dogpile on it because it makes them feel righteous. But if it's a game, these things actually matter: A) Is it fun? B) Does it look good? C) Does it LOOK like AI or have its own distinctiveness? People care about that, in that order, not whether some random stranger is "capable". Doing A B C is proof of the competence in the way that acutally matters. You could do it by hand and still fail most of them, so AI isn't the actual thing people care about.

There's a distinction between revealed and stated preferences. Most people will say "I'm against AI for content" in the abstract, but their revealed preferences show they still consume, read and share it if the content is good when noone is there criticizing their choices.

replies.author: sarmatianheroes
replies.body:
I can understand the similarities at first glance, but there are quite a few fundamental differences in gameplay:

* Heroes have a maximum level of 6. Leveling up unlocks additional army slots rather than increasing attack and defense.
* Hero skills develop through actual use rather than automatically through leveling.
* Unit positioning plays a much bigger role. Units standing next to each other can form defensive formations, while archers positioned together can perform area attacks through combined volleys. There are also mechanics to counter these formations.
* Some units can transport others, such as the Trojan Horse or Roman Siege Tower.
* You build your own cities, including walls, gates and defensive towers, and later fight battles inside the cities you've designed.
* Artifacts introduce new gameplay mechanics rather than simply increasing hero stats.
* There's no magic, and each historical faction has its own unique mechanics and technological development.

My goal is to make the game less dependent on randomness and overpowering hero statistics, and more dependent on tactical decisions, unit positioning and army composition.

I'm deliberately keeping some familiar Heroes mechanics because I don't see a reason to change things that already work well just for the sake of being different. :)

replies.author: Actual-Finish2672
replies.body:
1K of images may be a lot to draw, but as someone who appreciates the work that goes into a vision even if the skills aren't quite up to the task, there are ways around it.

So yes, the AI art sticks out and brings several concerns to mind about the rest of the game. A lot of issues I see is most people over design if they're using AI to accelerate the process and may end up with bloated game that lacks a clear vision (though it does seem you didn't fall down this trap)

Usually the benefit of having a longer dev cycle while making the art is you can refine the gameplay while you work though you've mentioned this is solo so that can feel daunting. It helps to make a spreadsheet of all required artwork and where it's used. If you're good with using AI, ask it to compile a spreadsheet of all sprites with the sprite, where, and how they're used. Then you can see which ones may be redundant, not used, and devise a plan to efficiently redo them (granted at this point with how large it is, might be good to finish and go to the next project with mindfulness of how much art is needed)

Two last things:

1. For future projects, try to choose art styles that you can achieve/want to practice. You'll never know what you can do if you don't try and practice.

2. For games like this with the pre-rendered isometric characters, usually you would do them efficiently by making 3D models then setting up camera rigs to keep a consistent angle. Again, may be pretty hard to redo all the art now, but something to keep in mind for future projects.

replies.author: sarmatianheroes
replies.body:
Thanks for the constructive feedback!

I actually worked in game development long before generative AI existed, collaborating with artists on mobile games. From my experience, finding artists who can consistently deliver the required volume of assets, maintain a coherent visual style and meet deadlines isn't particularly easy.

Regarding your second suggestion, that's actually how I'm making the units. I use 3D models, animate them manually and render them into 2D sprites using a custom rendering pipeline to maintain consistent camera angles and lighting.

I'm also gradually moving more environmental assets and buildings to the same pipeline to improve visual consistency.

The main challenge here is the sheer scale of the project and finding a realistic way to finish it as a solo developer without compromising too much on my original vision.
